subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) points out that eating is one of them. Let us be under no illusions. This is not a Bank Act, unfortunately, which is antithetical to the interests of the banks. This is a Bank Act in a sense which simply in the mildest way possible attempts to say to the banks that they cannot have absolutely everything they are asking for; there are some limitations on the market power the banks are going to be allowed to exercise. In our view the limitations are very important but not as large as we would have liked them to be. Nevertheless, they are necessary.
In the case of automobile dealers, as has been pointed out by other speakers, why in the name of goodness should we allow the banks to get into the business of leasing cars? Why should that become a part of the business of banking? I feel equally strongly, as do other members of my party, about a very successful, growing-I am speaking of what it will be like ten years down the road-and increasingly important sector, the data processing sector and the computer industry dealing with payroll, accounting and a number of financial services which are provided to business. In our view the banks must be very carefully and strictly regulated in that field.
Mr. Macintosh mentions it as being one of the most important sectors, and he urges that they be allowed to continue to stay in this field. We are not happy with the regulations which have been put forward by the Department of Finance because we feel that those regulations give too broad a power to the banks and do not give sufficient protection to a growing Canadian industry. The answer always given by the banks to these criticisms is that they can provide the best and most competitive system and that all that we are doing by giving an advantage to credit unions or to the automobile dealers or to the data processors is subsidizing inefficiency. That is their argument. Their argument is that the wider public interest will be served by the provision of the most efficient and least expensive service. On many occasions when Mr. Macintosh has presented this argument before the committee-and I would like to leave this argument on the record in terms of our perspective-I have said that the public interest is not simply defined by having one, two or three large and extremely powerful financial institutions providing every single kind of financial and economic service to the consumer. In the short run that may provide a cheaper service, but one also has to ask whether the elimination of whole sectors of our economy, the takeover of smaller Financial institutions and the removal of all the market power and ability of small businessmen in the car-dealing field and in the data processing field is really in the public interest. Would it not be in the greater public interest to have a diversity of institutions providing information and services to the consumer, and should we not be striving in our

November 7, 1980
Bank Act
Bank Act, as I have said, to provide for a degree of government involvement and regulation which guarantees the protection of the consumer in one instance and a genuinely competitive system with trust companies, caisses populaires and credit unions providing competition with the banks on the other? With regard to this last point, 1 think there is another major illusion. Introducing the foreign bank provisions of this act, as hon. members know, allows foreign banks up to 8 per cent of the total assets of Canada's banking system. The argument has been made that this is one key way of allowing for greater competition in the system. We can look at the difficulties faced by the Continental Bank and we can look at the amendments presented by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) with respect to small banks and their reserve requirements. We agree with those amendments, because if we are to provide for a genuinely competitive system and in fact encourage the growth of smaller Canadian banks, then in a sense we must give some market advantage to those groups. If we are genuinely concerned with this problem, then it may well be that the government reserve policy will have to be sufficiently lenient and discriminating-I am not saying discriminatory, 1 am saying discriminating-to allow for the growth of banking institutions which will provide for perhaps more specialized services to particular sectors of the economy, but subject to federal control and regulation, with guarantees of at least ownership being fairly widely dispersed and so on.
As we know, foreign banks will very quickly get to the 8 per cent limit. Indeed, to my regret I predict the House will be requested by the government to increase that limit during the life of this act. The implication is that foreign banks will come in and take over the business of foreign subsidiaries of companies working overseas. In a sense they will skim off that business from current Canadian banks. Having, in a sense, occupied that 8 per cent, we will not be in a position to encourage the formation of smaller Canadian banks, whether they be the Crown banks which our party discussed in committee, trust companies or other financial institutions which decide to become banks.
In summary, there are two main problems with the Bank Act before us. It does not recognize the need to increase the power of the government to regulate the banking industry, and, to be polite, it provides for insufficient protection of the public interest. For example, it indicates that there will never be Crown banks, that no public servants can serve on the boards of directors of banks, and that banks will continue to be allowed to set whatever interest rates they wish without any intervention by government. Those are all examples of inadequate protection of the public interest. Also the act fails to provide for real and genuine competition, from the points of view of other institutions, other industries and consumers.
In closing I should like to refer to one amendment-I know the minister has stepped out of the House for a moment, but I have spoken to him about this many times. I know there are other members of the House who are equally concerned with the principle contained in the amendment. If the government
rejects all the principles of consumer protection and financial disclosure-they have accepted some but rejected others- they should think again about the following item. I am referring to the fact that we do not require banks which are engaged in over 35 per cent of their business overseas, in substantive and major dealings with foreign countries and the agencies of foreign countries to inform the Canadian public on an annual basis as to the number and size of their loans. The principle of confidentiality has been abused to prevent consumers and other various interested groups from knowing exactly the foreign policy of our banks. We have many examples of where it would be useful to know the domestic policy of our banks. For example, if the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce lent the amount it is reported to have lent to Massey-Ferguson, it is no longer a matter of confidentiality. It becomes a matter of concern to the governments involved in the negotiations, to consumers concerned about where they will bank, how they will bank and the wisdom of carrying out policies where such a large share of assets is tied up by one company. If the domestic policy is unsatisfactory, the foreign policy implications are tremendous.
All our banks are engaged on a day-to-day basis with loans of a huge size to countries all over the world. When this happens it has implications for Canada's foreign policy and those people who are deeply concerned about the internal policies of those governments. I am referring, for example, to the governments of South Africa, Chile, Eastern Europe and cases where internationally syndicated loans are arranged through large companies.
I see Mr. Speaker about to rise to his feet. This is one amendment which the government could well accept without for a moment moving away from the basic principles contained in the act. In fact it would merely extend principles already accepted in committee, in other words that, there is a right to know on the part of every consumer and an obligation on the part of these companies to divulge all their financial information on as full and fair a basis as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my confusion I thought the minister would speak before me but if he wishes to close the debate, that is fine.
I wish to turn to the second half of my stint this afternoon and deal with amendments 1 and 2. I think it is quite clear that the House should have a clarification of what I have in mind for motion No. 1, which is the definition of a bank.
November 7, 1980

1 have been astounded over the past many years, first of all during the revision in 1966 when the then minister of finance, Mitchell Sharp, and the then Inspector General of Banks refused an invitation to define the business of banking. At that time the act did not use the phrase "business of banking" as it does in this present version. As a lawyer it seemed to me incongruous that here was an act containing prohibitions against anybody setting up as a bank, yet they refused to define a bank in that act. In commercial practice as a lawyer, when clients came in and asked what they could or could not do under a statute, I took one look at the statute and told them that the limitations on the business contemplated was this or that. That is the purpose of a statute. Now we have one of the most important statutes in this country before us, one that is singular in that it has a sunset period. It is an act that defines what can and cannot be done. But it refuses to define what a bank is. It merely says that a bank is a bank under the act. Perhaps it is a secret among the bureaucracy. I cannot understand it, nor can my lawyer friends, whether they were members of the committee or witnesses before it.
1 have a whole series of references to testimony given by those appearing on behalf of the Canadian Bankers' Association and many others. I know the governor of the Bank of Canada privately would love to have the definition. He says: Well, we are getting along without it, so why rock the boat? Of course, the governor of the Bank of Canada could not criticize the government on this point.
When clients come in to see a Canadian firm of lawyers and say they want to carry on a business and want to know if we will be deemed to be a foreign bank, they set out their operations. Then we look to the definition of what is a foreign bank. On page 4, at line 39, we find the definition of "foreign bank". It says:
"foreign bank" means a corporation, association, partnership or other institution incorporated or established by, pursuant to or in accordance with the laws of a country other than Canada, or a department or agency of the government of a country other than Canada or a political subdivision of such a country, that
(a)	is a bank according to the laws of any country other than Canada where it carries on business.
Presumably the law of that country of incorporation will be sensible enough to determine what a bank is. We, in Canada, cannot do it. The definition, under (b), continues:
(b)	carries on a business in a country other than Canada that, if carried on in Canada, would be wholly, or to a significant extent, the business of banking,
We ask: what is the business of banking? At present in Canada a lawyer would have to say to his client: I cannot tell you because there is no business of banking defined in this act. As Canadians, we cannot tell you what our Canadian Bank Act defines as the business of banking. I find that extraordinary, Mr. Speaker.
I now move to section 6 of the act, in which the government compounds the nonsense of the absence of a definition of the business of banking in the clause which extends the life of this act. Section 6 appears at line 21 on page 13 and says:
6. (1) Subject to this act,
(a) if Parliament sits on at least 20 days during the month of March, 1991, each bank may carry on the business of banking until the first day of April, 1991, and no longer;
Bank Act
In subparagraph (b) there appears the phrase "business of banking" but there is still no definition. Then we go to section 302, which deals with foreign banks. I am reading from page 306 at line 4:
302. (I) A foreign bank shall not, directly or indirectly,
(a) undertake any banking business in Canada,
Mr. Speaker, I invite you to enlighten me and to tell me what that means when there is no definition provided as to the business of banking. I suppose one could resort to that Solomon-like statement attributed to a judge of the Court of Appeal in Manitoba who was reported to have said: Banking?
Is that what bankers do? The Supreme Court of Canada in a recent case involving the Canada Labour Code and a trust company decided that since the trust company was not a bank it did not fall under the provisions of the Canada Labour Code-banks come under the Canada Labour Code but trust companies do not. That is the sole distinction as to the business of banking.
I do not know how many times I have done this, but again I am moved to refine it further-and I am not wedded to the words themselves. If anybody can come up with better phraseology they are welcome to try. I would submit to hon. members that we can get around this problem here by defining what is meant by a bank. I am susceptible to all of the political weak-kneeism and wet-noodle-backbone attitudes that may have been expressed by the federal government in the past, and at the present time, when they refuse to face up to the proposition that money and banking is under their exclusive federal jurisdiction. But some provincial governments, because they have incorporated trust companies or financial companies-just merely incorporated them-say they have jurisdiction over their operations. My foot, they have! Provincial governments incorporate aircraft companies, broadcasting companies, grain companies, but they do not have a thing to say about their operations. Therefore, these provincial governments should have nothing to say about near banks and their operations within the field of money and banking. The provinces have waltzed in and, shall we say, by default on the part of the federal government, have gone into the field of money and banking to the extent that chartered banks now only have 65 per cent of their money on deposit. Thirty-five per cent of the money on deposit is outside the purview of the bank, when the constitution says that 100 per cent should be within its purview.
Credit unions are incorporated. They can be incorporated under provincial legislation, but once they step into the business of banking they are in the area of federal control. Similarly, if a co-operative engaged in the business of aircraft wanted to fly its own plane, it would have to apply to the federal government for licences for the aircraft, for its air worthiness, for radio transmission and all the other purposes of operating that aircraft. So why should a credit union engaged in the business of banking not be subject to the same regulations or similar regulations under the Inspector General of Banks?

Although the credit unions do not share that view, it is my view. The credit unions have a number of advantages. When the credit unions began, they were not nearly as strong as they are now. One of their strongest pleas for some of the advantages they now hold was that they were the small man's bank, that they were there in lieu of mortgage companies, trust companies and banks. Strangely enough, credit unions now have their own mortgage company, trust company, and I hear they have now formed their own auto leasing company.
Now that the banks have been pushed out of auto leasing, the credit unions have stepped in. The whole point of removing the banks from that industry was to protect the automobile dealers because it attacked the heart and soul of their business. It was not for the benefit of credit unions. I am sure hon. members on the government side have never heard of this development. Certainly there was no letter written or word given to any member in the official opposition with regard to that particular development. I am not trying to fault the credit unions, I am merely trying to illustrate the lack of logic.
I say that a bank means, (a) any financial institution engaged in the business of lending money and accepting deposit liabilities transferable by cheque or other instrument or, (b) any financial institution engaged in the business of lending money raised in Canada through the acceptance of deposit liabilities or the issuance of securities, but does not include any financial institution incorporated as a credit union, caisse populaire and federations of such or any other co-operative credit society. So I have grandfathered them. That should satisfy those people who feel credit unions should operate under exclusive provincial control even though they are engaged in the business of banking.
A bank also means, (c) any financial institution subject to the Quebec Savings Banks Act. That is perfectly right because we have an act to cover that situation. Next, a bank is any financial institution wholly owned by the federal or provincial governments or treasury branches or offices thereof. There is the Ontario Savings and Loan Association and there are the Alberta Treasury Branches. There may be some other institutions of which I am not aware which would be covered under this particular exception.
A bank is any financial institution incorporated as an insurance company within the meaning of the Canada and British Insurance Companies Act. Again, that is just to make sure that somebody inadvertently does not get caught up as a bank. Finally, I say that a bank is any financial institution incorporated either federally or provincially as a trust company, mortgage and loan company or a finance company with more than 75 per cent Canadian ownership and where no foreign individual or associate individuals or groups own more than 10 per cent of the voting shares.
I made that particular exemption deliberately because that last paragraph would catch foreign banks operating in the country in a great number of cases because the only exemption is for companies or institutions incorporated federally or provincially as a trust company, mortgage and loan company or finance company. There are a number of trust companies
which are subsidiaries to American banks as well as banks of other countries. The finance company Finance America is a subsidiary of the Bank of America. I refer to companies which have more than 75 per cent of Canadian ownership because that is what we insist on for our Canadian banks. There would be a limitation of 10 per cent for any individual or associated shareholder.
That is what we require of the Canadian banks and, yet, I find an inexplicable reluctance on the part of the government to accept this amendment. Logically, the minister does not have a leg to stand on because there is no lawyer who will say that this is a sound piece of legislation. The legislation insists on using the term "bank" and "business of banking" but refuses to define that term. I have defined it and I am satisfied with the definition. I invented the definition with a number of groups and they themselves say the language is good. Somebody may find something better, but I defy any lawyer or any member of the government side to tell me that in an act like the Bank Act one does not require a definition of the "business of banking".
How would the government advise a client as to what is permissible to a bank and what is not permissible to a bank? This is a point upon which I insist that I am right. I know some people say I get pretty tenacious about some of my own opinions, but this has been consistent, and many of the members of the committee privately share my point of view. I also know that this point of view, that one must define banking, is shared by many people on the outside.
One has to define banking. How are we going to assist the federal court or the Supreme Court of Canada in deciding matters under the Canada Labour Code if we refuse to define banking, if we refuse to define what institutions are banks and which are not banks? Therein lies the jurisdiction.
Then there is the matter of the case in Manitoba. Does the minister feel the judgment of the court there resolved the problem in any way when the judge said that the business of banking is what bankers do?
I most earnestly urge the House to consider this amendment and that which follows. One says what a bank is, and the other one says that the business of banking is that carried on within the meaning of this act as defined.

Mr. Speaker, there are two views of what we can do, one of which has been stated by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) in his amendments. The other is the view of the government.
The view of the government is that basically, we define the general field of banking by virtue of the act but, because of the difficulties of attempting to find a definition of a bank which is under federal legislation-and this is the whole constitutional problem which lies behind this difficulty-beyond that, there is no need to set out a precise definition of banking and that in
November 7, 1980

fact to have a precise definition would cause more problems than it would solve.
1 simply want to refer the minister to the case to which the hon. member for Edmonton West refers, Computer Services Limited and Comcheq Services Limited versus the Toronto Dominion Bank which was decided by Mr. Justice Monnin in the decision for the majority of the Court of Appeal on November 22, 1979. 1 am afraid I do not have any other citation for that case. I only have the original of the decision. As the minister is no doubt aware, this case is under appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.
The difficulty that I think Mr. Justice Monnin's decision gives rise to is a very real one-and this perhaps speaks directly to motion No. 2 proposed by the hon. member for Edmonton West. The judgment of the trial court was that banking is what banking activity is described as in section 75 of the old act. But Mr. Justice Monnin is saying, no, that is not true. The judgment reads in part:
I do not think that this is a correct statement of the law. Parliament never intended to establish a fixed or restricted definition of banking by enumerating clauses (a) to (d) of section 75. Banking must have a much broader meaning.
It goes on to say:
All the textbook writers on banking confirm this statement that there is no exact definition of a banker or a bank. In fact and in practice, banking is what banks do for the carrying on of their business; what they do can vary from decade to decade and from century to century.
He goes on to find that the computer payroll service and something called the "compucount" which is a kind of accounting service provided by the Toronto Dominion Bank in the city of Winnipeg, is something that banks do, and therefore is part and parcel of the business of banking.
The amendment, motion No. 2 proposed by the hon. member for Edmonton West, may seem unnecessary. Some members may ask, what is the big deal? Because it simply reads as follows:
'business of banking' means that business carried on in whole or in part by a bank within the meaning of the act.'
There is a real difference between that concept of the business of banking, the concept contained in the judgment of Mr. Justice Monnin, and, if I understand the position of the government, the philosophy that in a sense underlies the new act; that is, that banking is what bankers do; that there are specific prohibitions contained in the act which prevent bankers from doing certain kinds of things but apart from those specific prohibitions there is no limitation on what a bank can do.
For the reasons which 1 outlined earlier with respect to the market power of the banks, the effect of new technologies on smaller companies and the banks' tremendous ability to use these new technologies and introduce them in ways that might not have been anticipated, I think it is better for this Parliament to err on the side of limitation. In other words, it is better to have a specific prohibition in the beginning of the act which says that banking is what bankers are allowed to do under this act and nothing else, rather than to follow the broader concept
Bank Act
of banking contained in the judgment of Mr. Justice Monnin and contained, I think, in the general thrust of the legislation.
The hon. member for Edmonton West mentioned a number of examples. I want to refer to clause 174(2)(j) which deals with data processing services. It seems to me that unless we have a definition at the beginning of the act which limits banks to specific services provided for in the act and nothing else, that it is precisely in a field such as data processing that we will find the banks, judging from speeches as the one made in Toronto on November 3, by Mr. Macintosh, becoming active.
I want to indicate in a general way that we are in favour of the principles of the amendments presented by the hon. member for Edmonton West because unless we restrict the definition of banking to what is specifically allowed in this act on a ten-year basis, we are giving a blank cheque to the banks to engage in all sorts of activities which we may not anticipate in this year, 1980.

I see Professor Pepin smiling; I trust 1 am not stretching my sophisms to the extent of troubling his Thomis-tic mind.
We have adopted the aspect of the definition that is functional. We say: a bank is an institution which, either through letters patent or incorporation, can operate within a specific framework. In part V, on page 164 of the bill, banking business is said to be the operations and powers of the financial institution known as a bank under the first definition. 1 feel "therefore" that the object of the concerns of the hon. member for Edmonton West is covered, though not covered in the same way. It is not done as rigorously as the hon. member would have it, precisely to avoid the obvious pitfalls on the constitutional level. That is why 1 move that the House reject motions Nos. 1 and 2.

To this end, the bill would empower the Canadian Radiotelevision and Telecommunications Commission to require the necessary contractual arrangements to be worked out between stations and networks on the one hand and authors and artists on the other.
We have had considerable correspondence over the last eight years with regard to this bill. We have had federal government support for allowing schools to obtain these educational films, but we have met with very limited success.
I have had correspondence from the following schools, universities and others across Canada supporting this bill and asking the federal government for help: The Prince Edward Island Teachers' Federation; the St. James-Assiniboine School Div. No. 2 of Winnipeg; The Board of Education for the city of North York; the River East School Division of Winnipeg; the Manitoba Teachers' Society; the Canadian School Trus-

tees' Association; the Niagara South Board of Education; School District No. 63 (Saanich) Sidney, B.C.; the Separate School Board of Metropolitan Toronto; The Manitoba Association of School Superintendents; Brock University, St. Catharines, Ontario; the Canadian Teachers' Federation; the School Trustees' of Greater Victoria, and the University of Alberta. As well, individual teachers and school trustees have asked for assistance in having the subject matter passed to committee. The Canadian School Trustees' Association has written to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) asking that this bill or the subject matter be referred to committee.
After years and years of discussion about the use of television programs in our schools and universities, it is time interested groups, such as the Canadian Schools Trustees' Association, teachers associations and other groups be permitted to come to the committee where the problems on all sides can be ironed out.
In a letter from the Canadian School Trustees' Association to the President of the Privy Council, it is stated:
For eight years, the bill has been considered and always voted out; but only because of the usual procedures of the House with respect to private members' bills that originate outside of the government. The bill has never had real consideration before a committee of the House, even though we have good reason to believe that members of all parties in the House would normally be prepared to support the bill. Seven years ago, there was an opportunity made available; but even though we brought people from across the country to appear before the committee, the meeting of the committee lacked a quorum because of traumatic events in the House; and we were never heard, including others, such as representatives from the Canadian Teachers' Federation.
The government said that if I withdrew the bill, it would allow the subject matter to go to committee. It went to committee. School teachers and school trustees from across Canada came to the meeting, but no Liberal members showed up, which I found most insulting. 1 hope we are not going to have similar treatment here this afternoon for Canada's educational system.
We are now making a special appeal to have the bill go before the committee again so that all concerned can make their views known to members of Parliament for a judgment based on more information.
The letter from the Canadian School Trustees' Association continues:
Progress has been made in Great Britain and the United States toward off-air taping of programs for educational, non-profit use; but here in Canada, we are still at square one. Students in the classrooms are the real people affected; and this is regrettable at a time when taping off-air privileges could have a significant impact on making students more aware of their own country.
It seems very little to ask to have the bill or the subject matter go to committee. Also, the executive director of the Canadian School Trustees' Association, Mr. C. H. Witney, has written a letter to the Secretary of State (Mr. Fox) in support of the bill or the subject matter to being referred to committee. States consisted of representatives from the major networks, unions, guilds and education. That is what we are asking for in Canada but we are at a standstill.
1 have further comments from interested parties. The advisory committee of the Toronto Metropolitan Separate School Board, in a brief prepared for the director of education, says the bill "would bring a welcome extension to the use of video tape recordings in our school system." In their brief they state:
-"radio or television program intended as part of the curriculum of elementary or secondary schools . . ." may eliminate some excellent programs. The program "Man Alive" would be excluded by this definition and yet it is the program most frequently requested for video taping. Also, to deny the video taping of newscasts would restrict teachers who could use this as part of the curriculum. For example, in the grade 9 history course the topic of French-English relations is taught and there would be useful information contained in newscasts.
Serious legal problems have arisen for some schools across Canada and proceedings have been instituted against 14 CEGEPs, that is post-secondary educational facilities in the province of Quebec. They are being sued by a group representing artists and producers. The suit attempts to recover $990,000 for the illegal reproduction of audio-visual tapes. The CEGEPs are being sued for institutionalized fraud, and it is obvious that changes to the copyright legislation are necessary. The best place to discuss these changes would be in committee.
I see we have the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) here this afternoon who, I understand, will be bringing in some changes to the copyright legislation. I hope he will be introducing this legislation shortly as it would certainly assist our schools in obtaining educational films. School divisions in British Columbia and Manitoba have also been threatened with lawsuits, Mr. Speaker, so you can see that it is time we came to their rescue.
In July, 1975, in Britain the BBC and the ITCA permitted schools and other educational institutions to record educational programs off-air for later use in schools. It was necessary for these two agencies to make appropriate arrangements with certain performers, unions and holders of other relevant rights. This was not thought to be an insurmountable problem for the networks, school authorities and the government of the United Kingdom. I think it is a problem we in Canada can solve with just a little effort, the first step being the referral of this bill to committee for further study. I hope we will receive a favourable response from the government this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, my party and I tend to support the bill in principle. We would like to see it go to committee for further discussion, and we hope members on the other side will not see fit to talk it out, for a very good reason.
First, it is a very important piece of legislation which could potentially improve the scope of education in the schools and colleges of our country. Second, I do not know how many members realize how greatly the use of video tape recorders has spread. I have some statistics here which show the prolifer-

November 7, 1980
Broadcasting Act
ation of these machines. They are not really confined to homes, radio stations or television stations. They will be used in schools and other institutions, and they are already. So what I am saying about the hon. member's bill is simply that the use of apparatus of this kind is going to spread and copies are going to be made of intellectual properties anyway. They are being made at present and there is nothing that we or anyone else can do to stop this technological advance. It is unstoppable. It is somewhat akin to the technology associated with satellites and earth stations, and we will have to adjust our legal system to become more consonant with the new technology. If we do not do that, what will happen is that we will see a tremendous growth in this kind of under-the-table illegality which already has occurred with print material where you have a vast amount of copyright material of "someone's intellectual property", either that of the creator or of the publisher. At the moment, schools and colleges are running these off by the hundreds on Xerox machines and on various types of ditto machines, and publishers and various other companies which have some rights so far as these properties are concerned are at a loss to know what to do.
Certainly there is occasionally an attempt to bring a suit, to make an example of some institution or of some individual, some school teacher or high school bandmaster who wants another second flute part and Xerox's copies from the original. It is precisely the same thing as will occur now with different material in the video taping. The recorded form, for that matter, is also something that has been going on for some years. People have been taping recordings for years. With this sort of bootlegging or private taping, nobody, neither the publisher nor the composer or creator, gets any kind of benefit.
Surely if it is done in other countries, it is not beyond our intellectual capacity to make some kind of arrangement, as we have with the radio stations through CAPAC and BMI, for a performing rights fee based on the volume of the radio station or the percentage of his gross. It does not seem to me to be impossible to work out a system of fees and charges which could apply to institutions so that the publishers or the owners of those rights could get something out of it. You might as well legalize it and organize it rather than allow it to go on and proliferate in an illegal, pirate way as it is today.
Certainly it is complex, extremely complex. Although this bill mentions only the Broadcasting Act, what is involved more deeply and more intimately is the copyright aspect. The hon. member did mention that. The Copyright Act amendments are something we tried to bring in here in 1971 when the present Madam Speaker was not yet a member of Parliament. I recall first meeting her at the deliberations of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs when it was studying Bill S-9 which was attempting to ask for copyright amendments so that performance fees could apply to the replay of records on radio stations. The idea was that the money would go to the composer and the publisher, but the performer himself on a "hit" record, if he was a back-stop musician, would get some benefit. That attempt failed ultimately, and the minister then became minister of state partially responsible for the Copyright Act, or
closely associated with the minister who was responsible at that time. Nothing has happened since in that regard. There are complexities here, but if other countries could solve this problem, it seems to me it would not be beyond Canada's ability to do the same thing. I therefore support the hon. member's representation and hope that it goes to committee so that it can be thoroughly examined. I do not think there is any threat to anybody's ministry or anybody's ego in this thing. There should be more of this kind of non-partisan examination of issues such as this, which are not associated with any political party, in an attempt to solve a particular problem faced by groups of institutions and hundreds, if not thousands, of young people.
Let me give the House some indication of the growth in the past four years of these video tape recorders or cassette recorders. There are many of them. There are different types, but that is not important at the moment. I am quoting from The New York Times Magazine of August, 1979. It says the following:
But in the past four years, hundreds of thousands of viewers have acquired video cassette recorders (VCRs). By plugging a VCR into their television sets, people can record any program they choose for later viewing. Firms such as Sony and Matsushita (which distributes its VCRs through (RCA) dominate the American market, and their cassette machines are being exported from Japan-
And get this, Mr. Speaker.
-at the rate of 100,000 a month.
It goes on to say how these things are used. Sure, they are used in homes. They are going to be used in schools. They are used in schools. Video casette players are available to schools, colleges and individuals, and they are now down to the price of $400 each. It is estimated that by 1988 there will be a penetration in the homes of the United States to the extent of 40 per cent.
We are dealing with this matter now, and no amount of stalling or foot-dragging will change anything at all. All we will do is make criminals or illegals out of many people who through their own honest efforts will attempt to use the new material and technology. I really do not want to become involved with some sort of conflict with the law.
I congratulate the hon. member for putting this motion forward. I congratulate members of the government and the minister for listening so attentively and politely. I hope I have made some contribution. I hope I have given the House a glimpse of the immensity of the problem and also the immensity of the challenge. I support wholeheartedly the hon. member's bill as well as his request that we have a look at this in committee, because it needs to be done.

Let us look at the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie). He gave us a long list of people who support his ideas. Included in the list were teachers, college professors-all consumers. There were no writers, no artists, no producers, no designers and no publishers. Copyright exists for very specific reasons. It exists to protect property and to ensure that people will get recognition and payment. The book industry, newspapers, the music industry, arts and films take copyright laws very seriously because all these people own their material, and they want payment for it. They want protection against its misuse, and they want recognition of their own artistic and creative inputs. When we come along and try to exempt people from copyright laws, we are taking away from the creators of those materials the rights they quite properly now enjoy.
As I mentioned, I have experience in book publishing, and I have seen this happen time and again. I remember a case in British Columbia in which the teacher's federation Xeroxed an entire book and then sent copies to the publisher. I remember in my own publishing company specifically putting on a map the information that the customer could Xerox the map but that the rest of the book was protected from such reproduction. As we look at the arguments of the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine, we find the same ideas being discussed around more and more sophisticated technology.
The hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) was quite right in saying that this technology is spreading, but he was wrong when he inferred that we should condone the practice that is spreading with the technology. Because the bootlegging is happening, in his opinion we should okay it. Car theft is happening as well. Should we okay that? We did not okay horse theft, and when the technology improved we did not okay car theft. We could use the same parallels here. In this bill we are asking artists and writers to subsidize municipal taxpayers. We are saying that schools and colleges do not have enough money to afford materials which they somehow justifiably deserve, and so the writers, publishers and designers, those who spent their time, their thought, their intellect, their money and their labour, are the people who should subsidize the taxpayers. And that harsh fact is hidden by dragging in legions of small children and earnest teachers who somehow deserve access to this material free or cheap.
Broadcasting Act
I am sympathetic to the idea that we need more money for educational materials at all levels of our school system. I am also sympathetic with people who succumb to temptation because the technology is there and it is easy to reproduce the material. But I also know, despite my sympathy, that these are quite separate issues, and I feel determined that we should be protecting the people who give us the materials in the first place.
It should be clear that the right to take away property is not the correct route to raise cash for our school systems. I do not think the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine would voluntarily give away half his back yard because somebody wanted to build a new school next door and did not have quite enough room. He probably would not give away his car if the school needed a new bus. And we should not ask people to give away their films, their newspapers, their paintings or their books just because enough cash cannot be raised this year from local taxpayers.
In fact, if we look at the consequences of the sympathetic approach the hon. member has taken, we will see that it is actually counterproductive. Perhaps in the short term he would have more materials than he could reproduce on his VTR or on his Xerox, but in the long term he would have fewer materials. Who would do anything remotely useful for a school if it was likely to be stolen from him at the school? We would find-and this pattern has been occurring in book publishing and it would occur again in films and television-that people would somehow just avoid servicing the school market because they would not be getting a proper return for their labour, their investment and their thought.
I congratulate the hon. member. Everyone wants good schools. In fact, I have a niece and a nephew who attend schools in his riding, and I am most anxious that they be good schools. We all want ample materials in those schools, and again, because of my family ties, I want very good materials in the schools in his riding. The people to whom we should be talking are not the artists or the producers. We should talk to Mr. Sterling Lyon and tell him to quit cutting taxes and to supply the schools properly.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

That is where the money comes from, not from the producers. If the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine takes the long-term view and does some homework, he will find out that it is really an old argument. He can go all the way back to the days of Mark Twain and find that some of his books were actually pirated and published in Canada before they appeared in the United States. The fact that it was done in the days of Mark Twain was a strong enough argument for Canada eventually to set up good copyright laws. I do not think we should start backing away from that now just because we have new machines and it is easier to infringe. We should remind people that if they will not steal a physical piece of property, they should not steal an idea. Instead, we should take the sentiment in this bill and redirect it.

When the Secretary of State and Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) comes here and asks for more money for some of his good programs to help creative people, we should give him that money. When the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) comes here and asks for more money to create markets, we should give him those opportunities. When our artists and producers come to us asking for protection and recognition, we should respond to their requests as well. When we and the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine start doing this, we will find in the long run that there are cheaper and better materials in the schools.

I am pleased Mr. Speaker did not recognize me before the hon. member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher), he added a dimension to this discussion which has not hitherto been presented on eight occasions since the motion first appeared on the order paper and went through its annual pilgrimage in the House. Obviously the hon. member is a lobbyist for the book publishing business. We have not had the benefit of that interesting viewpoint until now.
We are faced with a real problem, and I do not think any perspective should be accepted as the only one. I express admiration for the manner in which the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) sponsored this bill. He introduced it reasonably and has persisted over eight years in bringing it before the House. 1 have had a similar experience in sponsoring a private member's motion for almost as long to set up a committee on the disabled. Finally we have achieved our goal in that regard. We are working very constructively and creatively in a non-partisan manner to deal with the problems of the disabled community.

speechtext:
That is something we were not able to obtain before. I hope hon. members heard the statement of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). We have been attempting to get some action in the area of transportation for the disabled. This is good news that we have received this afternoon.
The sponsor of this motion is only asking that it be referred to a committee. It must be referred to a committee. We have heard the viewpoint of publishers expressed by the hon. member for Mississauga North, the viewpoint of the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) who is a teacher with many years of experience, and the very constructive presentation of the mover of the bill.
The tragedy is that this matter was referred to committee on a previous occasion, but because of the exigencies of the
business of this House, there was no quorum in the committee and it could not proceed with its business. As the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine said, there were no Liberal members present at the committee. Whether that was deliberate or due to circumstances, we do not know. But, he received the approval of the House and of the government, and let us hope it is renewed before we finish our discussion this afternoon.
We are living in a time when information is expanding explosively. This phenomenon has been occurring for the last 30 or 40 years. Actually we were much better off in making audio-visual information available to educational institutions a couple of decades ago than we are now. In the past two decades we moved into the area of television communication and now we are moving toward Telidon communication. In the not too distant future everyone will have a machine in their homes through which they will be able to communicate with the community and the world at large. This invention is sponsored by the Government of Canada. The government has not yet sorted out the politics arising from this new magnificent technology, and what we are discussing today is a step in the right direction, if the subject is allowed to go to committee.
What will we do when Telidon is developed by the Government of Canada in collaboration with the private sector, Northern Telecom? We will be able to sit in our homes and bring in information of all kinds. What will the book publishers do about it? Telidon will have access to library resources all over the country, to satellite information, to electronic funds transmission, to electronic mail transmission and the whole business. This technology will require major changes in existing legislation and will result in the implementation of various new pieces of legislation. The bill before us is only asking for a reference to committee where we can grapple with one small segment of the total picture.
Obviously the hon. member for Mississauga North has not read the bill; his speech must have been prepared for him. If he had read the bill, he would have realized that clause l(vii) on line 26 reads:
-provisions respecting royalties payable to such authors or performers-
The whole idea is to make contractual arrangements. This is the emphasis of the bill. It would make it possible for royalty provisions to be payable to authors and performers. There is no desire to steal, as the hon. member for Mississauga North implied. There is no desire to steal or to avoid the necessity of making a reasonable contribution. This is what is being done now, as the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody told us. When Telidon comes on-stream it will be done in every home. It is to regularize and legalize what is already being done.
I say we have gone backwards in this regard. When I was in the educational field there used to be some interesting activities designed to inform the citizens of Canada, through audiovisual means, of some of the great events that were taking place at that time. This kept Canadians informed on current affairs. The two programs of which 1 speak were "Citizens
November 7, 1980

Forum" and "Farm Forum". These were sponsored by the CBC and excellent information was published by them and distributed. The National Film Board supported this educational activity by establishing a network of film councils across the country. These films were available free of charge. They were films on all sorts of topics of educational value to the schools, colleges and universities of this country. This service is no longer available because of the advent of television. Canada has not come to grips with that problem. As a result, our students and our citizens are being deprived of a very important and necessary source of information. The United States are ahead of us in this regard. They have the Public Broadcasting Service which is privately-funded and doing an excellent job of providing educational programming. It makes the programs available to schools and educational institutions. The CBC could do this, as it used to do with "Citizens Forum" and with "Farm Forum", backed up by the audio-visual services of the NFB.
I want to make one further point. I have already made reference to the fact that it took eight years to get some action on behalf of the disabled community by bringing a motion repeatedly before this House. I hope we will have the same response from the government spokesmen this afternoon who will rise and say: Yes, let it go to committee because we have a real problem here.
I also hope that the government will move quickly in the area of copyright because copyright provisions at the present time make it impossible to serve our schools and universities with audio-visual material. This also applies in the area of the disabled. Some radio stations have tried to provide a reading service for the blind and visually impaired. They cannot provide such service. They are willing to provide the service but they cannot do so because they are prevented by antiquated copyright legislation. Let us move forward in this direction. Let us see what can be done to change our out-dated copyright regulations so that urgently-needed services of the audio-visual educational kind can be provided to our schools. I mention this particularly for the benefit of the member for Mississauga North, so that publishers, writers and creators can be adequately compensated. I am sure there is no one, no author, no creative person in this country who wants to deny the young people of Canada in the schools the benefit of what they have created.
This bill is asking for amendments to the legislation which will make it possible to provide the royalties. Let us move forward in that area. Let us move forward in the area of copyright. Hon. members know that the government has, in the past decade or so, been talking about this for almost as long as amendments to the Bank Act have been talked about. Let us do it. Let us move this excellent piece of legislation into committee and get on with solving this urgent problem. New situations, new circumstances and new legislation will be required in order to come to grips with the impact of the revolution in technology-as Alvin Toffler calls it, the "new wave".

Mr. Speaker, I take the floor, first, as the member for Mercier and, second, as former chairman of a regional school board and present trustee of the same school board. I would remind my hon. colleague from Winnipeg-Assiniboine that 1 shall be meeting my colleagues tomorrow at which time I shall have the opportunity of consulting them in that regard.
However, after having been active in the school system for five years, this is the sixth year of my term, I must say that this bill in no way meets the needs of Quebec school boards, and 1 am surprised that a Manitoba colleague can introduce a bill that trespasses on so many rights, individuals and bodies. In any event, 1 think this bill, as we say in French, is "stuffed" with good intentions, but as hell is also, "stuffed" with good intentions, I doubt that is the purpose of this bill.
1 must also remind the House that, in this bill, we deal with a matter that falls under the jurisdiction of the Superior Council of the Ministers of Education, which means that we are dealing directly with a matter of provincial jurisdiction. As far as I know, and with regard to the allegations of my colleague for Winnipeg- Assiniboine, I have not heard that the ministers of the superior council made any request to the effect of changing our federal laws to authorize them to glean so-called educational programs from both public and private television networks. However, I see that my colleague extends the matter to television programs in section 3(2), which I quote:
-and any television program dealing primarily with history, science, the arts and current affairs, but does not include a newscast.
In other words, almost 90 per cent of all television programs produced can be used and taped by the minister of education network.
I believe my colleague and other hon. members would be well advised to see just what is now available to the ministers of education in the field of educational films. With this in mind, I brought my colleague for Winnipeg-Assiniboine a repertory of films on the penal code, published by the department I represent as Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada.
Now it would have access to hundreds of films and refer the said document to the Manitoba Department of Education and make available to thousands of young people an extremely well prepared documentation from various sources at some ridiculously low prices and often free of charge. However, I do not intend obviously to give a lecture on the excellent films produced by the National Film Board of Canada which come under the jurisdiction of the federal government and which also make available to school boards some high quality films also at set prices or even free of charge. Therefore, I think that school boards are very well served by the Canadian govern-

November 7, 1980
Broadcasting Act
ment as far as the production of educational films is concerned.
I wonder about the basic subject matter of Bill C-224, a bill practically authorizing the broadcast of all television programs throughout Canada. The member did not put any limitation in his bill about the programs originating in the United States since it is rather easy to gain access to the American production in Canada. Therefore, in my opinion, while the bill is full of good intentions, it does not surely attain the objectives sought by the member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie).
Furthermore, as a school trustee and as a member sitting on a school board in my riding and accountable in another riding for another school board to which I have sent the reference book 1 mentioned earlier, 1 must say that I am surprised that there could be so much interference with the rights of all the people involved.
In fact, I am thinking of the authors, namely, the people who created those television programs; I am thinking of the producers and all the teams who participated in the production of those programs. I am not questioning the judgment of school boards in selecting programs which could be of some interest for those students. However, I believe it is not within the federal government's jurisdiction to initiate such action and to make available to the provinces material qualified as school and educational material, without their specific request.
Besides, I find it rather strange that a Progressive Conservative colleague normally so concerned with the welfare of private enterprise should propose now an almost socialist oriented bill. In fact, mention is made in this bill to cover rights which have been respected and if they have not been respected as they should, as mentionned by the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) I do not see why we should try to make legal things which are being done illegally at the present time and if there is any need for putting teeth in the law I think that would be the right course to follow rather than making things legal by interfering with the basic rights of artists and authors. In fact, Mr. Speaker, in the arts, as you no doubt know, it is extremely difficult for an artist to become known, to earn a living, to have a decent income in order to feed a family and in the long run to enjoy a decent living as a Canadian citizen.
What the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine suggests, is for a federal control over television broadcasts and to offer them at a reasonable cost. I am sorry, but I do not think that it is the responsibility of the Canadian government to set a reasonable price for those broadcasts. At the present time, I believe that most of the programs shown on televison networks are available to all provincial governments which may, if they wish, obtain copyrights in order to show these programs in educational broadcasts. Therefore, I do not see how a member of the Progressive Conservative Party could allow such government interference in private business or in matters which come under the jurisdiction of another level of government. In fact, although I have not inquired about the situation in Manitoba, I know very well what services are offered in Quebec and in Ontario with regard to educational broadcasting and I must say that in Ontario the programs are of excellent quality. Not only does that province have access to Canadian productions but there are exchanges with countries of the European community, on a regular basis. Furthermore, beside those exchanges, the Ontario and Quebec governments have made joint efforts to produce educational programs, to which quite often participate our national radio and television network, but which are initiated by the provincial governments and which come under their own jurisdiction.
So, I do not see why my colleagues are up in arms on a constitutional motion which does not temper with provincial jurisdictions and I do not understand how a bill may be brought to the floor of this House, and have such an impact in a field which is strictly under provincial jurisdiction.
Mr. Speaker, coming back to article 2(4) which states: "Notwithstanding the provisions of the act on copyright, copy, retention and utilization of a broadcast in the expected way, are deemed not to constitute infringements on copyright".
I protest, Mr. Speaker, such a clause which makes it possible to infringe upon copyrights. We know, as my colleague from Mission-Port Moody said earlier, that protecting copyright is no easy task and since that problem is to be tackled, I think the government will not hesitate to adopt such a measure. However, I think it is rather strange that a party so concerned with individual rights, a party which loathes social legislation, a party whose philosophy has always been based on the individual, should deny this very individual, who is the author, the opportunity to discuss his own copyrights, to set up his rights himself to negotiate them freely with television stations as well as denying him the opportunity to pass contracts involving retransmission.
By the way, the provinces can now have access to the whole Canadian government production through the educational network, for a nominal cost or for an amount which covers only the technical cost of production. Therefore, it seems very odd that such a provision be included in a bill which is supposed to aim at child education.
I must say that if my colleague is so concerned with the education of his children in his province, I offer him to share with the director of educational services of Le Gardeur School Board, on which I still sit, as a matter of fact, all resources which we have as regards bibliographies and films which could be put to the disposal of school-boards. Besides, I must say that as productions are made both in English and French in Quebec, his province would surely benefit from their use.
In addition, I have not heard the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine say in his speech that he had consulted
November 7, 1980

organizations as important as the Union des artistes or any other union concerned by the matter, and I believe that in such an important area, this is one of the basic things which must be introduced if we want such a legislation to take form and become statute.
On the other hand, 1 turn to the assertions of my colleague who was speaking earlier about Telidon, advanced technology, the opportunity to broadcast all kinds of documents through television. I do not think this government which has precisely presided over in the technological innovation in the telecommunication field, which, finally, has spent for many years huge amounts on research in this area, should deny the opportunity to use such advanced technological tools.
However, in spite of gossips and scandal-mongers, I must say that this government is anxious to respect members of the education superior board, their needs, their viewpoints, and if the latter make application to acquire such aids, 1 suggest the Liberal government could sit down and discuss the matter. But 1 believe that this legislation, as a matter of fact, represents a considerable infringement not only in the right of provinces, not only on the right of individuals, but it doesn't trust those who assume responsibility in this area.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, if I had to sum up the matter, I would say that this legislation is paternalistic in a way. As a matter of fact, it would like to dictate conduct to school-boards and tell them how to use their educational aids and where to find them. Finally, credit would certainly be last where credit would be due. Personally, speaking this time as a mother of three children, Mr. Speaker, I can confirm the findings of Statistics Canada, namely, that children are spending by far too many hours watching TV, and that all those who are interested in the issue, whether as teachers, psychologists or associated specialists, are indeed very concerned about this situation.
[DOT] <1700)
Before introducing such a bill and instead of allowing the students to have access to more hours of television under the pretext of education, we should perhaps look for innovations more in agreement with personalized education, with a type of
Broadcasting Act
education where the child is no longer treated as an object, but rather as a human being.
Mr. Speaker, the technology of television can be used well, and I believe that certain provincial governments-since I cannot give a summary of the situation throughout Canada- are now putting educational television to very good use. However, it is not by making available hundreds of hours more of programs that we can solve the problem of education for Canadian children. I believe that, at the present time-and my colleague can correct me if I am wrong-we have all the technical material that we need and the problem of education is not related to a lack of educational books or of technological aids available to school boards, but rather to the values and the system itself, to the children in our schools who have been ignored in the last few years and treated as numbers.
Mr. Speaker, we have tried in our school-board to give back to our students a quality of school life which is concerned less with the teaching environment and the quality of the building itself than with the quality of the teachers and personal contacts with each student, which aspect has been somewhat ignored in recent educational reforms.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-224 pretends to be aimed at education but, in fact, it only represents interference by the federal government in an area which comes nearly completely under provincial jurisdiction. Mr. Speaker, I cannot support such a bill since I believe that by restricting this action to educational television, we would be opening the door to much greater dangers. Indeed, my colleague must know that we have throughout Canada community television stations which could also claim the same rights and say that, to educate the public in general, they want to take over these programs, and this would provoke a chaos which would benefit no one.
